stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 4: Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Wednesday said the American people had rejected war, claiming that the outcome of the US midterm elections reflected public opposition to the conflict with Iran. “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X, according to Iran’s IRNA news agency. “If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added. Ghalibaf’s remarks came as results/projections from the US midterm elections showed the Democratic Party winning control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, dealing a major setback to US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. The Democratic victory is expected to make it more difficult for Trump to advance his legislative agenda and could intensify congressional scrutiny of his administration’s policies, including its handling of the conflict with Iran.

stories.headline: Trump admits war in Iran, oil prices led to poll loss; but says would 'do it again'
stories.title: Trump admits war in Iran, oil prices led to poll loss; but says would 'do it again'
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 05: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said it was “largely true” that the war in Iran cost the Republicans heavy losses in the midterm election, but struck a defiant note, saying he would do it again as it was the “only answer” in the “long term”. "Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," Trump told reporters when asked about Vice President J D Vance’s remarks that the Iran war led to Republican losses in the election. "But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said. The president insisted that the US would have done nothing different as far as the war was concerned. "But I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different. We've totally broken their military. The navy's gone. Their air force is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone," Trump said. “The Iran thing, we had to do, and we continue to do it. We have tremendous oil flowing out of the Hormuz Strait now. At the beginning, there was none. And, probably that's the primary reason – the price, not the war, the price (of oil),” Trump said. The president also said that he was not considering replacing Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, despite public dissatisfaction with the war with Iran. Hegseth is “doing a great job", he said. Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump's likely successor at the White House, blamed the president's war in Iran for Republicans' midterm wipeout.

stories.headline: Iranians celebrate setback for Trump in US election, and other Mideast news
stories.title: Iranians celebrate setback for Trump in US election, and other Mideast news
stories.summary: Dubai, Nov 05: Iranian officials were emboldened by a stinging election setback for US President Donald Trump, and world leaders waited to see whether Washington would end the war with Iran. Meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed they fired strikes on an airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh. The Israeli military said it struck two suspects in Lebanon, killing one person. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Wednesday. Read our full coverage here. Iran’s leaders say election shows US voters rejected Trump’s war Iranians celebrated on Wednesday after US voters, concerned about the war and frustrated over rising prices for fuel, gave Democrats control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote — a major blow for Trump and his Republican Party. Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, wrote Wednesday on X that “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” He warned that if the US government ignores the vote for change, “it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.” But Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, dismissed thoughts that the US will change its approach to the Islamic Republic. The broader region has been on edge for weeks over whether the US will resume full-scale military operations against Iran. Talks are ongoing aimed at preventing renewed fighting. Underscoring the mutual hostility, thousands marched through Tehran on Wednesday at a government-organized demonstration commemorating the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy. Pro-government demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” UN peacekeeping chief says Lebanon needs UN presence and urges a Security Council decision Jean-Pierre Lacroix said Wednesday that Lebanese officials fear a “security vacuum” between Israeli forces and the Lebanese army when the UN peacekeeping mission known as UNIFIL ends December 31. Lacroix, who recently returned from the Middle East, warned of the risks of leaving the two armies “sort of face-to-face” without a third-party presence. He questioned who would monitor the U.N.-drawn Blue Line separating Israel and Lebanon, prevent unintended clashes and support communities in southern Lebanon. The border region patrolled by UNIFIL has experienced decades of violence, including a full-scale war between Israel and Hezbollah militants in 2024. Israel has long accused UNIFIL of failing to prevent Hezbollah from building up its military presence along the border. Lacroix said efforts to disarm Hezbollah had failed because “there was no political will.” The United States, Israel’s closest ally, successfully pushed the U.N. Security Council to end the mission after nearly five decades. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres proposed three options in June to maintain U.N. monitoring along the border. Lacroix said unarmed UN military observers would still be authorized to operate in southern Lebanon but questioned how they could do so without protection or support. He said a Security Council resolution adopted in 2000 remains in effect. The council is scheduled to discuss it Nov. 19. Houthis claim strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia In Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday claimed without providing evidence that they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh as well as several areas in southern parts of the country. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said rebels fired a ballistic missile toward the airport, causing what he described as “major damages” to the airport. He also claimed that the group fired a drone at a radar installation and a ballistic missile at a command and control center in the Jazan province. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify these claims. The Saudi information ministry didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The Saudi civil defense issued an alert in Riyadh overnight and other warning alerts of potential “danger” in Jazan and Najran early Wednesday. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted oil and logistic facilities as well as airports in Saudi Arabia as part of their plan to fight what they describe as the kingdom’s “blockade” on Yemen. 7 killed in airstrike in Yemen, Houthis say At least seven people, including two children, were killed in an airstrike Wednesday in Yemen’s southwestern province of Taiz, Houthi health authorities said. The Houthi-run health ministry said in a statement the strike hit a house in the district of Maqbanah and also wounded six other children. The Houthi media aired footage it said was of the struck building. The footage showed a heavily damaged concrete building, with large sections of the roof and walls collapsing. The ministry blamed Saudi Arabia, which didn’t immediately comment on the accusations. It was the latest deadly strike in Yemen since the country’s civil war was revived more than three months ago. The fighting pits the Iranian-backed Houthis against Saudi Arabia and its ally, Yemen's internationally recognized government. Israeli drone strike on southern Lebanon In Lebanon, the Health Ministry said the strike on a motorcycle in the village of Qabrikha killed one person and wounded another. The Israeli military said in a statement that it had “struck two suspects who were observing IDF soldiers” without providing further details. The attack was the first in nearly a month as such drone strikes have been rare since a US-brokered ceasefire in late June ended the latest Israel-Hezbollah war.

opening: Seoul: A meeting between Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appears increasingly unlikely when the US president travels to Asia in November, analysts say, after he suffered a crushing midterm election defeat.
Trump had said he "may" meet Kim this month and that it "would be exciting", but appeared to backtrack in October, saying, "I don't know...
body: I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting," while adding that his "relationship with Kim Jong Un is very good." Trump's focus on Kim and his scaling back of joint US-South Korean military drills have alarmed Asian allies, while sparking speculation that he is seeking a foreign policy win as his war with Iran stalls.

But Kim's powerful sister Kim Yo Jong signalled on Wednesday that there was little appetite for renewed dialogue with Washington, saying Pyongyang had "no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons"." The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us," she said.
Kim Yo Jong's comments came after the FBI accused North Korea of a $6 billion heist from cryptocurrency exchange Binance -- allegations she had previously slammed as "a grave political provocation".

Kim's statement marked "a shift from defence to offence", said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies in South Korea." The latest statement uses the (cyberattack) issue as an opportunity to condemn the entire US policy of pressure against North Korea," he told AFP.
In 2019, North Korea's Kim Jong Un made a 60-hour train journey home from Hanoi empty-handed after a summit with Trump collapsed.
Now, the dynamic has reversed.
Trump is making repeated overtures, only to be met with reluctance from Pyongyang." For Kim Jong Un, maintaining the status quo is the best option right now," Lim said.
Weakened TrumpAnalysts say the North Korean leader has even less incentive to meet Trump after his Republican party suffered a thumping defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3.
But Washington's "divided government and Trump's lame-duck status will be an important variable for North Korea".

Pyongyang will be sceptical of Washington's ability to deliver lasting concessions, said Michael Bosack, founding director of the Parley Policy Institute and a former UN Command official." The Kim regime is looking for substantial and durable changes in US policy towards North Korea.
Right now, nothing Trump offers comes with a guarantee that it will last beyond January 2029," Bosack told AFP, referring to the date when the US president's second term ends.
Kim's deepening ties with Russia and China have also strengthened his position and reduced his incentive to engage with Washington.

North Korea's economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, Seoul's central bank estimated in July, citing Pyongyang's "expansion of economic cooperation with Russia" as its major driver.
Nuclear ambitionsEven if Trump and Kim agree to meet, their differences over North Korea's nuclear weapons programme remain a major obstacle to any breakthrough.
Pyongyang has repeatedly made clear it is no longer prepared to discuss denuclearisation.
Kim Yo Jong said in September that the country's nuclear-armed status was "absolute", calling those hoping for denuclearisation "idiots".

It came as South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung -- who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions -- suggested Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North's nuclear programme and offer sanctions relief in return.

That approach would face significant obstacles following Trump's midterm defeat though, with Democrats committed to denuclearisation and Congress holding powers over sanctions relief." Pyongyang retains negative memories of failing to make progress in negotiations under the Biden administration because of its position that there would be no sanctions relief or dialogue without prior denuclearisation measures," Kyungnam University's Lim said.

North Korea's distrust of Washington, coupled with the uncertainty surrounding any agreement with Trump, could boost its nuclear ambitions." North Korea's belief that independently advancing its nuclear arsenal, regardless of changes in US administrations or political parties, was the right and strategically sound decision will be further reinforced," Lim said.

Pyongyang has carried out a flurry of weapons tests in recent weeks, including trials of cluster-bomb warheads, attack drones, a precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile." The development, testing and training of new weapons will become regular and routine activities," Lim predicted.

stories.headline: Questioning Democratic Institutions
stories.title: Questioning Democratic Institutions
stories.summary: The Congress party's relentless campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls exposes a familiar pattern in its political conduct: questioning democratic institutions whenever their functioning does not suit its political narrative. A party that has spent years questioning electoral transparency and accusing others of undermining democracy now finds itself uncomfortable with an exercise designed to strengthen the very foundation of free and fair elections. For Congress, electoral reforms appear welcome only when they serve its political interests. When duplicate entries, deceased voters and questionable registrations are discussed by opposition leaders, they become legitimate concerns. But when the Election Commission undertakes a nationwide exercise to identify and correct such discrepancies, the same party raises the alarm and turns an administrative process into a political controversy. The Special Intensive Revision is not an exercise designed to benefit the BJP or any other political formation. Its fundamental objective is to ensure that electoral rolls reflect genuine voters, remove erroneous entries and protect the integrity of the democratic process. A clean electoral roll is the starting point of a credible election, and no responsible political party should oppose that objective. SIR is about cleaning electoral rolls, not deleting democracy The figures emerging from the exercise underline its scale and administrative effort. Across the states where SIR was undertaken, voters were provided between 100 and 158 days, or approximately four to five months, to complete the enumeration process. Of the country's approximately 95 crore voters, nearly 82 crore, accounting for around 88 per cent, submitted their Enumeration Forms. Approximately 13 crore entries were placed under the ASDD classification — Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate — during the preparation of revised electoral rolls. The reported figures included approximately 2.89 crore deceased voters and 1.01 crore duplicate entries. The remaining cases involved voters who were absent, had shifted or could not be traced during the verification exercise. These numbers demand serious attention. Electoral rolls cannot remain static documents carrying the names of people who have died, permanently shifted or registered at multiple locations. Such discrepancies undermine the credibility of elections and create avoidable complications in the voting process. The exercise involved extensive field-level verification. Booth Level Officers (BLOs), along with political party functionaries, reportedly made three visits to voters' residences to collect enumeration forms and verify entries. This was not simply an administrative exercise conducted behind closed doors; it involved extensive ground-level participation. Importantly, exclusion from a draft roll does not mean that a genuine voter has permanently lost the right to vote. Eligible individuals can seek inclusion through Form 6, subject to the prescribed verification process. stories.headline: PSA can’t bypass criminal law: HC
stories.title: PSA can’t bypass criminal law: HC
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 04: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has quashed the preventive detention of a Pulwama resident booked under the Public Safety Act (PSA), observing that extraordinary powers of preventive detention cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal proceedings or to bypass safeguards available under criminal law. The court directed the authorities to release Ajaz Ahmad Seh, a resident of Sehpora in Rajpora, Pulwama, forthwith, provided his custody is not required in connection with any other case or under any other lawful order. Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal passed the judgment while allowing a habeas corpus petition challenging detention order No. 34/DMP/PSA/2025 dated July 28, 2025, issued by the District Magistrate, Pulwama, under Section 8 of the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act. According to the grounds of detention, Seh was allegedly in contact with a Pakistan-based terrorist handler affiliated with Jaish-e-Mohammad through telephone and the encrypted application Zangi, accessed using a virtual private network (VPN). He was also accused of functioning as an Over Ground Worker (OGW) by allegedly providing food, shelter, clothing, transportation and information to active terrorists, including Haris Nazir of Kachipora, Rajpora. The police dossier further alleged that he shared information about the movement of security forces and encouraged local youth to join terrorist organisations. However, the High Court observed that despite the seriousness of the allegations, the detention grounds lacked specific particulars, including the dates of alleged communications, the nature of information exchanged and the particular acts through which logistical assistance was allegedly provided. The court held that merely asserting that a person used an encrypted application or remained in contact with individuals allegedly associated with terrorist organisations was insufficient, without relevant supporting material, to justify curtailing personal liberty through preventive detention. "Preventive detention legislation cannot be permitted to become an instrument for bypassing the safeguards of the ordinary criminal process," the court observed. It further said that if the investigating agency possessed evidence of electronic communications, assistance to terrorists or sharing of security-force movements, the allegations could have been investigated under applicable criminal laws, including the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, subject to the ingredients of the offences being satisfied. The court also questioned the District Magistrate's independent application of mind, noting that a comparison of the police dossier and detention grounds revealed substantial reproduction of allegations. It observed that the detaining authority was required to independently evaluate the material rather than mechanically adopt the police narrative. Citing Supreme Court judgments, including Rekha v. State of Tamil Nadu and Vijay Narain Singh v. State of Bihar, the High Court reiterated that preventive detention is an extraordinary measure and must be exercised sparingly and strictly within constitutional and statutory safeguards. "The Court does not minimise the seriousness of allegations involving terrorist organisations or activities prejudicial to the security of the State," Justice Nargal observed, adding that a balance must be maintained between national security and personal liberty. The court ultimately held that the detention order suffered from material legal infirmities and quashed it, directing Seh's immediate release, subject to there being no other lawful restraint on his custody.

stories.headline: Can’t become third chamber of Parliament: Supreme Court
stories.title: Can’t become third chamber of Parliament: Supreme Court
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: 'Can't interfere in norms for SC/ST seats in house'NEW DELHI: Refusing to blur the constitutional 'Lakshman Rekha' that separates the three organs of governance, Supreme Court Wednesday said it cannot usurp legislature's exclusive powers to interfere in the criteria for reserving an assembly or parliamentary constituency for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes." We cannot become the third chamber of Parliament," a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said while refusing to entertain a petition seeking quashing of a notification reserving Kadipur assembly constituency in UP for SCs.

The CJI-led bench said identification of constituencies to reserve them for SCs or STs was the sole prerogative of the legislature and the court could not interfere in it, and suggested the petitioner could resort to protests to make elected representatives take corrective measures.
The bench, which has been dealing with a large number of petitions on CJP protests, said in a lighter vein, "It is a good season for protest, dharna and 'naare baji'.

You can also raise your voice (in protest) and tell the elected representatives that time is ripe for revising the criteria of reserving constituencies for the SC community and adopt the principle of rotational reservation.
By approaching the constitutional court, you have dialled a wrong number.

"Appearing for a petitioner, senior advocate Gagan Gupta questioned the manner in which constituencies were geographically identified and reserved for SCs and asked whether "Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, can constitutionally operate in a manner which permits the same territorial constituencies to remain reserved for SCs over successive electoral cycles without any mechanism for periodic rotation".
The bench said, "Delimitation is a legislative exercise and the guidelines for carrying out that exercise cannot be tweaked by the courts.

Can the judiciary mandate the Delimitation Commission to adopt rotational reservation policy while demarcating constituencies for SCs?" The SC agreed with Allahabad HC, which had said that since Articles 330 and 332 provide for reserving constituencies for SCs and STs, no general candidate could claim that his right to contest from constituencies reserved for SCs and STs was violated.

article_sentences: NEW DELHI: Cabinet Wednesday approved a Rs 2,814 crore scheme to boost domestic processing of lithium and nickel, reducing dependence on imports of critical minerals.
PM Narendra Modi said India cannot afford to depend on other countries for processing such materials.
The scheme would encourage domestic investment and secure future supplies, he wrote on X.
Union ministry of mines said processing of critical minerals was concentrated in a few global locations.
The scheme aims to develop domestic processing capabilities, promote value addition and reduce import dependence by supporting processing facilities.
It targets processing lithium and nickel ores or intermediary products into high-purity compounds.
Cobalt is expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel production.

To be implemented until FY31, the scheme will provide a capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment for four plants: two lithium processing plants with minimum capacity of 30,000 tonnes each and two nickel plants with minimum capacity of 50,000 tonnes each.
The support will be capped at Rs 500 crore per lithium beneficiary and Rs 900 crore per nickel beneficiary.
Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, analytics and research (VISTAR) scheme the scheme with an outlay of Rs 4,371 crore will be spread over five years from 2026-27 to 2030-31.

To be implemented until FY31, the scheme will provide a capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment for four plants: two lithium processing plants with minimum capacity of 30,000 tonnes each and two nickel plants with minimum capacity of 50,000 tonnes each.
The support will be capped at Rs 500 crore per lithium beneficiary and Rs 900 crore per nickel beneficiary.

stories.title: US sanctions India-based couple, companies
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Washington: The United States has imposed sanctions on an India-based couple and several associated companies over their alleged involvement in facilitating Iran's shadow fleet through fraudulent maritime registrations and certifications, accusing them of helping sanctioned vessels transport Iranian petroleum and evade international restrictions.

Announcing the action on Wednesday (local time), US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Washington would take action against individuals and entities continuing to support the Iranian regime.
"As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us.
We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air," Bessent said in a post on X.
In a press release, the US Department of the Treasury identified the targeted individuals as India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his spouse, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid.

It alleged that the couple operated a network providing false flags and maritime certifications to sanctioned vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including ships operating on behalf of Iran's military and its proxies.

According to the department, Sharma and Shahid allegedly established fraudulent maritime registries and classification societies by creating websites that purported to offer services on behalf of countries that had not authorised them.
The Treasury said their activities dated back to at least 2014, when they allegedly attempted to impersonate the maritime flagging authority of the Caribbean nation of Dominica.
It further alleged that their network provided registration services to vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, enabling them to circumvent international restrictions.
Several India-based companies associated with the couple have also been designated, including Oceaniek Technologies India and Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited.

Other entities named include Precept Trends Private Limited, Polynesia Maritime Private Limited, Alexarya Finserv Private Limited, Alexarya Media and Entertainment Private Limited, Viharaboating Private Limited and Aryavart Maritime and Educational Trust.
The Treasury said the sanctions were imposed under Executive Order 13902, which targets key sectors of the Iranian economy, including petroleum, petrochemicals and aviation.
